sentences.text: Unescoceratops possessed the roundest teeth of all leptoceratopsids, a group of horned dinosaurs.
The generic name Unescoceratops means "UNESCO horned face" because the fossil was found in a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The specific epithet koppelhusae honors palynologist Eva Koppelhus, the wife of Philip J. Currie.
The only known fossil of Unescoceratops is a partial left dentary known as holotype specimen TMP 95.12.6, the specimen the species is based on.
The genus Unescoceratops was first described by Michael J. Ryan, David C. Evans, Philip J. Currie, Caleb M. Brown, and Don Brinkman in 2012.
Unescoceratops is classified as a leptoceratopsid and is the sister taxon to Gryphoceratops.
According to a cladogram proposed by Ryan and colleagues, Unescoceratops is currently considered one of the most advanced leptoceratopsids.
Unescoceratops lived during the late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 76.5 to 75 million years ago.
The time range recorded for Unescoceratops in the Paleobiology Database spans from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
